title: Music Theory
description: Read and understand the notes, scales, intervals, rhythms and chords behind the music you hear, and see why they fit together.
audience: A curious adult who listens to music and may play a little by ear or by chord chart, but cannot read notation or explain why a chord progression works. Needs arithmetic and counting only. No instrument required; a keyboard or guitar helps.
outcomes: You'll be able to read single notes on treble and bass clef and name them by pitch.
You'll be able to build any major scale and the three minor scales from their step patterns, and name a key from its signature.
You'll be able to name an interval by number and quality and work out its size in semitones.
You'll be able to count and notate rhythm in simple and compound metre.
You'll be able to build triads and seventh chords, label them with Roman numerals and explain common progressions and cadences.
You'll be able to spot parallel fifths and octaves and fix them in four-part writing.
You'll be able to describe the form of a short piece from its phrases and sections.

modules.title: Pitch and notation
modules.summary: What a note is, how pitches are named, and how notes are written on a staff.

modules.title: Scales, keys and intervals
modules.summary: The step patterns that make scales, the signatures that name keys, and the interval as the measure of distance between notes.

modules.title: Rhythm and metre
modules.summary: How time is divided into beats and bars and written down.

modules.title: Harmony, voice leading and form
modules.summary: Chords built from scales, why progressions pull toward home, how voices move together, and how phrases build a piece.

lessons.title: Pitch and the keyboard
lessons.objective: Name any key on a piano, count the semitones between two keys, and work out the frequency of a note an octave from A4 = 440 Hz.

concepts.title: Pitch
concepts.summary: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds, and it corresponds to the frequency of the vibration in hertz.

concepts.title: Octave
concepts.summary: Two notes an octave apart have the same letter name and a frequency ratio of exactly 2:1.

concepts.title: Semitone
concepts.summary: A semitone is the distance from one key to the nearest key above or below it, black or white; there are 12 in an octave.

concepts.title: Equal temperament
concepts.summary: In equal temperament each semitone multiplies frequency by 2^(1/12), about 1.05946, so 12 of them make a doubling.

misconceptions: Thinking an octave spans 8 semitones because it has 8 note names: counting letters A to A gives 8, but the keyboard has 12 steps between them. The name 'octave' counts the letters, which is why it misleads.
Believing equal steps in hertz are equal steps in pitch: 220 to 440 Hz is an octave, but 440 to 660 Hz is only a fifth, because we hear ratios and not differences.
Believing black keys are 'extra' or 'special' notes: they are ordinary semitone steps and the white keys' gaps are just uneven.
sequence: Start from the keyboard picture: 7 white-key letters repeat, grouped by twos and threes of black keys, which lets you find C by sight.
Define pitch as a heard property that tracks frequency, with A4 = 440 Hz as the current concert reference.
Show that each A in the keyboard doubles: 110, 220, 440, 880, 1760 Hz; name the octave as the 2:1 relationship.
Count semitones between neighbouring keys; show 12 steps between C and the next C.
Reveal that semitones are equal ratios (2^(1/12)), so the frequency of any key is 440 x 2^(n/12) for n semitones from A4.
Contrast with adding Hz: 440 + 220 = 660 Hz is a perfect-fifth-like step, not another octave.
examples: E5 is 7 semitones above A4: 440 x 2^(7/12) = 659.26 Hz in equal temperament (a pure 3:2 would give 660 Hz).
Middle C (C4) is 9 semitones below A4: 440 x 2^(-9/12) = 261.63 Hz.

figures.learnerAction: Tap a key to see its letter and its semitone distance from the highlighted C. (Audio would play the pitch when platform support exists.)

questionPlan.sample: How many semitones are there from C4 up to the next C?

historyNotes: ISO 16 fixed A4 = 440 Hz as the standard musical pitch in 1955 and it was confirmed in 1975; the A of an orchestra before that varied by place and decade.

lessons.title: The staff and clefs
lessons.objective: Read the name and octave of a single note on the treble or bass staff, including middle C.

concepts.title: Staff
concepts.summary: The staff is five lines with four spaces, and each line or space stands for one letter name; higher on the staff means higher in pitch.

concepts.title: Clef
concepts.summary: A clef fixes which line or space is which pitch: the treble clef curls round G4, the bass clef marks F3 between its two dots.

concepts.title: Ledger line
concepts.summary: A short extra line drawn through or beside a note head extends the staff, as for middle C.

concepts.title: Middle C
concepts.summary: Middle C, C4, sits on the first ledger line below the treble staff and the first ledger line above the bass staff.

misconceptions: Thinking the treble clef 'means' high and bass 'means' low in absolute terms: a clef is a lookup key and either one can write the same pitch.
Reading bass-clef notes as if they were treble-clef: the same line is a different letter and a different octave (the bottom treble line is E4, the bottom bass line is G2).
Counting ledger lines wrongly from the top of the staff: a ledger line is counted away from the staff in the direction of the note.
sequence: Open with a staff and one note; the same position gives different pitches depending on a clef.
Teach the treble clef from the G it circles (second line is G4), and the bass clef from the F between its dots (fourth line is F3).
Name lines and spaces going up in thirds: treble lines E G B D F, spaces F A C E; bass lines G B D F A, spaces A C E G.
Introduce ledger lines and place middle C in both staves; show the grand staff joining them.
Practice reading single notes by anchoring from a known note, not by reciting the mnemonic from the bottom each time.
examples: Treble clef: bottom line E4, then G4, B4, D5, top line F5; spaces F4, A4, C5, E5.
Bass clef: bottom line G2, then B2, D3, F3, top line A3; spaces A2, C3, E3, G3.
Middle C is on a ledger line below the treble staff and a ledger line above the bass staff, so one pitch has two spellings.

figures.shows: Treble and bass staves with one note head at a time and the clef fixed; no letter names shown.
figures.learnerAction: Click the letter name; the figure then reveals the answer with the anchoring line highlighted.

figures.shows: A grand staff with middle C written in both clefs.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the clef to watch the note move between staves while its pitch stays fixed.

lessons.title: Sharps, flats and the semitone
lessons.objective: Raise or lower a note with accidentals, spot where the keyboard has no black key, and give an enharmonic spelling.

concepts.title: Accidental
concepts.summary: A sharp raises a note by a semitone, a flat lowers it by a semitone, and a natural cancels an earlier sharp or flat.

concepts.title: Enharmonic equivalent
concepts.summary: Two spellings of the same key, such as F-sharp and G-flat, are enharmonic equivalents.

concepts.title: Whole tone
concepts.summary: A whole tone is two semitones; between neighbouring white keys it spans a black key, except at E-F and B-C.

concepts.title: Chromatic scale
concepts.summary: The chromatic scale uses all 12 semitones in an octave.

misconceptions: Believing E-sharp and F are different notes on the keyboard: they are the same key with different spellings, chosen by the key and the line of the music.
Believing every white-key neighbour has a black key between them: E to F and B to C are already semitones, which is why there are only five black keys per octave.
Thinking a flat is always a black key: B-flat is, but C-flat is the white key B.
sequence: Show a keyboard with 12 keys and ask what separates the pairs of white keys with no black key between them.
Define the semitone and whole tone by counting keys.
Introduce sharp, flat, natural and their symbols on the staff, including the rule that an accidental lasts to the end of the bar.
Explain enharmonic spelling as a naming choice, with a reason: spell a scale using each letter name once.
Count semitones along the chromatic scale as a ruler for later work.
examples: From E up to B: E-F is 1, F-F# is 2, G 3, G# 4, A 5, A# 6, B 7, so 7 semitones.
From F# up to C: G 1, G# 2, A 3, A# 4, B 5, C 6, so 6 semitones.
D-sharp and E-flat name the same key; C-flat is the same key as B.

figures.shows: Keyboard with every key labelled by white-key letter only, and brackets showing the semitone gaps at E-F and B-C.
figures.learnerAction: Drag a sharp or flat sign onto a key to see the resulting key highlight.

lessons.title: The major scale
lessons.objective: Build a major scale on any starting note from the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half, and name its degrees.

concepts.title: Major scale
concepts.summary: A major scale is seven notes built from the step pattern W W H W W W H, returning to the starting letter an octave higher.

concepts.title: Scale degree
concepts.summary: Each note of a scale has a number 1 to 7 and a name: tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant, leading tone.

concepts.title: Tonic
concepts.summary: The tonic is the first degree, the note the scale and key are named after and the one that feels like home.

misconceptions: Thinking the C major scale is 'the' scale and others are variants: all major scales share one pattern and C only avoids accidentals because of how the keyboard was drawn.
Believing a scale 'uses' only white keys: G major needs F-sharp, a black key, to keep the pattern.
Using enharmonic spellings freely inside a scale: each letter name should appear once, so D major has F-sharp and C-sharp, never G-flat and D-flat.
sequence: Play or show C major as the white keys and notice where the half steps fall (E-F, B-C), between 3-4 and 7-8.
State the pattern as steps, W W H W W W H.
Apply the pattern to G: G A B C D E then F-sharp then G, and see why the F-sharp is needed.
Apply to D and to E to build the habit; name the degrees and give the leading tone's pull to the tonic.
Preview the reason: scale-degree names will matter for chords in later lessons.
examples: G major: G A B C D E F# G (one sharp, to make the last step E-F# a whole tone and F#-G a half tone).
D major: D E F# G A B C# D (two sharps).
E major: E F# G# A B C# D# E (four sharps).

figures.learnerAction: Choose a starting note; place each arc yourself, then the figure checks the pattern and highlights errors.

figures.learnerAction: Compare two scales' brackets.

lessons.title: Intervals
lessons.objective: Name an interval by number and quality from two notes, and give its size in semitones.

concepts.title: Interval number
concepts.summary: The number of an interval counts letter names from the lower note to the upper note, inclusive, so C up to E is a third.

concepts.title: Interval quality
concepts.summary: Quality (perfect, major, minor, augmented, diminished) says which of the possible sizes the number takes.

concepts.title: Compound interval
concepts.summary: An interval larger than an octave is compound and is named by adding 7 to the simple number, so an octave and a third is a tenth.

concepts.title: Inversion
concepts.summary: Turning an interval upside down changes its number n to 9 - n and swaps major with minor and augmented with diminished, but keeps perfect perfect.

misconceptions: Counting the interval number by steps rather than letters: C up to E is a 3rd because there are three letters, not because there are two steps.
Using semitones alone to name an interval: C-G-flat and C-F-sharp are the same size (6 semitones) but a fifth and a fourth by letter, so they are diminished fifth and augmented fourth.
Believing perfect intervals have major and minor forms: only seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths do; unison, fourth, fifth and octave are perfect.
sequence: Count letters inclusive to get the number, then ask how many semitones that number should contain in the major scale built on the lower note.
Show the major-scale intervals above the tonic: 2nd 2, 3rd 4, 4th 5, 5th 7, 6th 9, 7th 11, octave 12 semitones.
Flatten a major interval by one semitone to make it minor; add or subtract one more to make augmented or diminished.
Introduce the inversion rule and check it by sizes (4 + 8 = 12).
Extend to compound intervals by subtracting 7 from the number.
examples: C up to E is a major 3rd (4 semitones); C up to E-flat is a minor 3rd (3).
E up to B is a perfect 5th (7 semitones); D up to F-sharp is a major 3rd (4).
A major 3rd inverts to a minor 6th: 4 + 8 = 12 semitones in total.

lessons.title: Key signatures and the circle of fifths
lessons.objective: Name the major key from a key signature, and the signature from a key, using the order of sharps and flats.

concepts.title: Key signature
concepts.summary: A key signature lists the sharps or flats of the key at the start of every staff, so they need not be written on each note.

concepts.title: Circle of fifths
concepts.summary: Going up a perfect fifth from C adds one sharp each time; going down a fifth adds one flat; after 12 steps you are back at C.

concepts.title: Relative minor
concepts.summary: The relative minor shares its major key's signature and starts a minor third (3 semitones) below the major tonic.

misconceptions: Reading the last sharp as the key: the last sharp is the leading tone, so the key is a semitone above it (three sharps F C G: the key is A, not G).
Thinking C major and A minor are different 'sets' of notes: they use identical notes with different homes.
Treating 15 key signatures as 15 different keys: C-sharp and D-flat share keys on the piano; the 12 sounds are spelled in 15 ways.
sequence: Show the staff with F-sharp: one sharp, G major. Add C-sharp: D major. Sharps accumulate in a fixed order, F C G D A E B.
Derive the order from the circle: each new sharp is a fifth above the previous one.
Turn it into a rule: the key is a semitone above the last sharp. For flats, the key is the second-to-last flat (order B E A D G C F).
Show the circle as a clock and count signatures by position.
Introduce relative minor as the note three semitones below the tonic.
examples: Three sharps (F, C, G): last sharp G, one semitone up, A major.
Two flats (B, E): second to last is B, so B-flat major.
Four flats (B, E, A, D): second to last is A, so A-flat major; the major key with 4 sharps is E; B major has 5 sharps.

lessons.title: Minor scales
lessons.objective: Build the natural, harmonic and melodic minor scales and say how each differs from the major.

concepts.title: Natural minor
concepts.summary: Natural minor follows the step pattern W H W W H W W and uses its relative major's signature.

concepts.title: Harmonic minor
concepts.summary: Harmonic minor raises the seventh degree of natural minor by a semitone, so the leading tone pulls to the tonic.

concepts.title: Melodic minor
concepts.summary: Ascending melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh degrees; the descending form usually returns to natural minor.

concepts.title: Parallel key
concepts.summary: Parallel keys share a tonic but not a signature, such as C major and C minor.

misconceptions: Believing A minor is a 'sad version' of C major: it shares C major's notes and differs in home and step pattern; mood depends on much more than mode.
Believing harmonic minor is a separate scale to learn from scratch: it is natural minor with one note raised.
Confusing relative and parallel: relative minor of C major is A minor, parallel minor is C minor, with three flats.
sequence: Start with A natural minor, all white keys from A: A B C D E F G A.
Read the steps W H W W H W W and compare with major.
Raise the seventh to G-sharp and show the augmented second between F and G-sharp (3 semitones).
Raise the sixth as well for melodic minor and explain why: smooth stepwise melody.
Make a map of relative and parallel minors.
examples: D harmonic minor: D E F G A B-flat C-sharp D.
E natural minor: E F-sharp G A B C D, one sharp.
C minor has three flats (B-flat, E-flat, A-flat); A harmonic minor has an augmented second F to G-sharp (3 semitones).

lessons.title: Rhythm and metre
lessons.objective: Count the length of notes in beats, read a time signature, and convert tempo to seconds.

concepts.title: Beat and tempo
concepts.summary: The beat is the steady pulse and tempo counts beats per minute, so one beat lasts 60 / bpm seconds.

concepts.title: Time signature
concepts.summary: The top number gives beats per bar and the bottom number gives the note value of one beat, so 3/4 is three quarter-note beats.

concepts.title: Note value
concepts.summary: A whole note lasts four quarter-note beats, a half note two, a quarter one, an eighth half a beat; a dot adds half of the note's own value.

concepts.title: Compound metre
concepts.summary: In compound metre each beat divides into three, so 6/8 feels like two beats of three eighth notes.

concepts.title: Syncopation
concepts.summary: Syncopation puts emphasis where the metre does not expect it, often by tying across a strong beat or by resting on it.

misconceptions: Reading 6/8 as six beats per bar: it is felt as two main beats, each a dotted quarter.
Thinking the bottom number is a count: in 3/4 the 4 names a quarter note, not four beats.
Thinking a dot adds a fixed amount: it adds half of the note it follows, so a dotted half is 3 beats and a dotted quarter 1.5.
sequence: Start with a steady click and show that tempo is just how often it clicks.
Build note values as halving: whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth.
Explain time signatures with bar lines and counting 1-2-3-4.
Add the dot and the tie, and rests.
Contrast 3/4, 4/4 with 6/8 as grouping into twos or threes, and finish with one syncopated bar.
examples: At 75 bpm one beat lasts 60 / 75 = 0.8 s, so a bar of 4/4 lasts 3.2 s.
A dotted half note is 3 beats; a dotted quarter is 1.5 beats, which is 6 sixteenth notes.
A bar of 6/8 holds six eighths, grouped 3 + 3.

lessons.title: Triads and seventh chords
lessons.objective: Build major, minor, diminished and augmented triads and the dominant seventh, and name the triad on each degree of a major scale.

concepts.title: Triad
concepts.summary: A triad is three notes stacked in thirds: root, third and fifth.

concepts.title: Chord quality
concepts.summary: A major triad is a major third plus a minor third (4 + 3 semitones), a minor triad 3 + 4, a diminished triad 3 + 3 and an augmented triad 4 + 4.

concepts.title: Diatonic triads
concepts.summary: Stacking thirds on each degree of the major scale gives major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished: I ii iii IV V vi vii-dim.

concepts.title: Dominant seventh
concepts.summary: Add a minor seventh above the root of a major triad and the chord is a dominant seventh, such as G B D F.

concepts.title: Chord inversion
concepts.summary: A chord is in root position when its root is the lowest note; first inversion has the third lowest, second inversion has the fifth lowest.

misconceptions: Thinking a chord's name is whatever its lowest note is: C E G over an E in the bass is still C major, in first inversion.
Using major scale degrees to guess quality: they alternate, so the triad on the 2nd degree is minor and on the 7th is diminished.
Believing 'major chord' means 'happy chord': quality is defined by the intervals, 4 + 3 semitones, whatever the context.
sequence: Take C E G: show the two stacked thirds and label them 4 and 3 semitones.
Alter the third and fifth to create minor, diminished and augmented; table the semitone sizes.
Stack thirds on every degree of C major using only its notes, and note the pattern of qualities; introduce Roman numerals (upper case for major, lower for minor).
Add a seventh to G to get G7, and say why it is called dominant.
Introduce inversions as the same notes with a different lowest note.
examples: F major: F A C. A minor: A C E. B diminished: B D F (3 + 3).
In G major, the triad on the sixth degree is E G B, E minor, so vi.
G7 = G B D F: major triad G B D plus a minor seventh F (10 semitones above G).

lessons.title: Progressions and cadences
lessons.objective: Explain tonic, subdominant and dominant function, name the standard cadences and write the chords of a progression in any major key.

concepts.title: Harmonic function
concepts.summary: Chords act as tonic (home, I), predominant (leaving home, ii or IV) or dominant (tension, V or vii-dim) and tend to move in that order.

concepts.title: Cadence
concepts.summary: A cadence is a chord pair that ends a phrase: authentic V-I, half cadence ending on V, plagal IV-I and deceptive V-vi.

concepts.title: Tritone resolution
concepts.summary: The third and seventh of V7 form a tritone, 6 semitones, which resolves inward to the root and third of I.

concepts.title: Leading tone
concepts.summary: The leading tone is the seventh degree, a semitone below the tonic, and tends to rise to it.

misconceptions: Thinking progressions are arbitrary: the pull of V toward I comes from the leading tone and the tritone of V7, not from custom alone.
Thinking V-vi is a mistake: it is called a deceptive cadence because it sets up the expected tonic and then substitutes the submediant.
Assuming the Roman numerals are in C: they are keyless, and I-IV-V in A major is A, D, E.
sequence: Take the dominant seventh G7 in C and point to B and F, the tritone.
Show how each resolves by a semitone to C and E, giving a strong close.
Group chords into tonic, predominant, dominant and check the common chain T-PD-D-T.
Name the four cadences by their last two chords.
Transpose a progression: I-V-vi-IV in G is G D Em C.
examples: In G major, V is D (D F# A).
A ii-V-I in C: Dm7, G7, C; I-IV-V-I in A: A, D, E, A.
V-vi in C is G to Am: deceptive.

figures.learnerAction: Place chord labels from a chosen key into boxes.

lessons.title: Voice leading
lessons.objective: Join two chords in four voices without parallel fifths or octaves, and say whether two voices move in parallel, similar, oblique or contrary motion.

concepts.title: Types of motion
concepts.summary: Voices move in parallel (same interval), similar (same direction), oblique (one holds) or contrary (opposite directions).

concepts.title: Parallel fifths and octaves
concepts.summary: Two voices a perfect fifth or octave apart that move to another perfect fifth or octave in the same direction sound like a single voice and are avoided in common-practice writing.

concepts.title: Common-tone retention
concepts.summary: Where two chords share a note, keeping it in the same voice makes a smooth join.

concepts.title: Voice ranges
concepts.summary: Soprano, alto, tenor and bass each occupy a range of about an octave and a half and should stay close.

misconceptions: Thinking the rule is 'never use fifths': fifths are fine; two perfect intervals of the same kind moving together in parallel are what the rule rules out.
Moving every voice to the nearest note of the next chord: smooth, but it may cause parallels, so the bass is usually the independent line.
Writing every voice by itself: voices must make sense together, not only as separate tunes.
sequence: Play four chords as four blocks and then as four lines, and notice the lines.
Define the four motions with arrows.
Explain why parallel perfect intervals reduce independence.
Move a progression: keep common tones, move other voices by step, move the bass for contrast.
Apply to V-I and to I-IV with a worked fix.
examples: Bass C3 to D3 with tenor G3 to A3: each pair is a perfect fifth (C-G, D-A) moving in the same direction, so parallel fifths.
Soprano E5 up to F5 with bass C3 down to A2 is contrary motion.
In V7 to I, B (leading tone) goes up to C, and F (the seventh) goes down to E.

lessons.title: Phrase and form
lessons.objective: Describe a piece's form from its phrases and sections, and count the length of a 12-bar blues.

concepts.title: Phrase
concepts.summary: A phrase is a musical thought that ends at a cadence, often four bars long.

concepts.title: Period
concepts.summary: A period is two phrases, an antecedent ending on a weaker cadence and a consequent ending on a stronger one, usually eight bars.

concepts.title: Sectional form
concepts.summary: Binary (AB), ternary (ABA), rondo (ABACA) and verse-chorus layouts describe how sections are arranged and repeated.

concepts.title: Twelve-bar blues
concepts.summary: The blues is twelve bars of I, IV and V chords: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I (or V).

concepts.title: Sonata form
concepts.summary: Sonata form has an exposition presenting two themes, a development that transforms them and a recapitulation returning both in the home key.

misconceptions: Thinking form is the same as genre: form is the layout and repeated sections, not style; a pop song and a Baroque dance can both be binary.
Counting bars by beats: a 12-bar blues in 4/4 is 48 beats, not 12.
Believing the recapitulation just 'repeats' the exposition: the second theme returns in the home key, which is the point.
sequence: Open with a familiar tune and mark where it breathes; those are phrases.
Pair phrases into a period and show the cadence difference.
Label sections with letters, and show the standard layouts.
Walk through the 12-bar blues in C: C C C C / F F C C / G F C C.
End with sonata form as the largest-scale example using the home-key idea.
examples: Blues in C, bar 9 is G, bar 10 is F, bars 11 to 12 are C.
A 12-bar blues at 120 bpm in 4/4: each bar is 2 s, so 24 s per chorus.
A rondo ABACA has five sections, with A returning three times.

courseCheck: A mixed check of: naming keys on the staff and counting semitones; building a major and minor scale from the pattern; naming intervals by number and quality with semitone size; reading a key signature either way round; converting tempo and note values to time; building triads and labelling them with Roman numerals in a given key; naming a cadence; spotting parallel fifths in a given pair of voices; and giving the form or bar length of a short example.
platformNeeds: Audio playback (a figure type 'audio_player'): synthesised tones for single pitches, intervals (melodic and harmonic), scales, chords, and a clickable rhythm pattern at a chosen tempo. The learner should be able to hear 440 Hz against 880 Hz, a major against a minor third, a V7 resolving to I. Use the Web Audio API with sine/triangle oscillators and a simple envelope so no samples are licensed. Without it every lesson still works through its svg_figure fallback, since no question in the plan requires listening.

Music notation figure ('music_staff'): render notes, key signatures, chords and rhythms on one or two staves from a compact text spec (ABC or MusicXML subset), with click-to-answer note heads. The svg_figure fallbacks hand-draw these.
Interactive keyboard ('piano_keyboard'): clickable keys that report letter, octave, semitone distance and equal-temperament frequency, and can highlight a scale or a chord.
Circle of fifths explorer with draggable pointer showing signature and relative minor.
Optional later ear-training questions ('choice' answered after audio plays): identify an interval, chord quality or cadence by ear. Not in the plan until audio exists.
